slides: Welcome back. In this part the prime questions get harder, and almost every one of them starts the same way, break the number into primes. Before the questions, one more tool that none of them teaches, perfect squares.

slides.say: A perfect square is a whole number times itself, like nine, which is three times three, or a hundred, which is ten times ten. So when is a number a perfect square? Let's look at its primes. A hundred is two squared times five squared. Both exponents are even.
Why even? A hundred is ten times ten, and each ten brings one two and one five. So the primes come in pairs, one copy from each ten, and every exponent is even.

Now fifty. Fifty is two times twenty-five, so two times five squared. The two has exponent one, and that's odd. So fifty is not a perfect square. And really, seven squared is forty-nine and eight squared is sixty-four, so fifty sits between them.
So here's the rule. In a perfect square, every exponent is even. And if even one exponent is odd, it's not a square.
Here's the classic question. What's the smallest k so that forty-five times k is a perfect square? First, break forty-five. It's nine times five, so three squared times five.
The three has exponent two, even, fine. The five has exponent one, odd. So the five is missing one copy, and k has to bring it. k is five.

Let's check it. Forty-five times five is two hundred twenty-five, and that's fifteen times fifteen. Ten times fifteen is a hundred fifty, and five times fifteen is seventy-five, together two hundred twenty-five.
Now careful, a lot of students take k as forty-five, to make forty-five squared. That's a square too, but it's not the smallest. The smallest k brings only the missing primes.
